clue.text: Coffee morning? Trail round with small child in tow

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the word for trail is read from its end

blocks.note: to stalk is to trail or follow quarry
CH is the short form of child

explanation.surface: A parent drags a toddler round the village to a coffee morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trail' here is the verb, to follow, and CH is the standard abbreviation for child; 'in tow' puts it at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A klatsch, from German Kaffeeklatsch, is an informal gathering for coffee and gossip; the question mark flags the loose fit.

clue.text: Squaw weaving cloth OK

indicators.note: weaving interlaces threads, so these letters are worked into a new pattern

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Native American woman approves of the cloth she is weaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weaving' belongs to the scene as the woman's work but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Klootch, from Chinook jargon of the Pacific Northwest, means a Native American woman, the dated sense of squaw.

clue.text: Large plate, antique: one'll feed sixty

indicators.note: feeding into something means going inside it

blocks.note: LX is sixty in Roman numerals
an means one, as the indefinite article

explanation.surface: One big old serving platter is enough to feed sixty guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feed' suggests dining from the plate, which fits the picture; here it puts one word inside the numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A lanx was a large flat dish or platter used by the ancient Romans.

clue.text: Alternative to bellows, maybe, woman raised with jerks

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising a word lifts it bottom to top, so it reads backwards

blocks.note: mort is old slang for a woman
physical jerks are exercises, physical education

explanation.surface: A woman jerks her arms up to blow the fire instead of using bellows.
explanation.walkthrough: Physical jerks is the British name for keep-fit exercises, hence PE.
explanation.definitionFit: A trompe is a device using falling water to drive a blast of air into a furnace, doing a bellows' job.

clue.text: For Pierre, his beloved restrained in panic her extravagance

indicators.note: restrained in means held inside, so the letters sit within the next words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of panic, all of her and the start of extravagance

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's sweetheart is made to rein in her panic buying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For Pierre' marks the answer as French; chère is the feminine of dear, used of a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Chère is French for dear, so a Frenchman would call his beloved his chère.

clue.text: Composer pockets schilling, coin put inside his new coat?

definitions.text: coin put inside his new coat?

indicators.note: to pocket something is to take it inside, so the composer holds the other piece

blocks.note: George Frideric Handel, the baroque composer
S is the abbreviation for the Austrian schilling

explanation.surface: A composer slips a foreign coin into the pocket of his new coat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'pockets' literal; it puts S into HANDEL.
explanation.definitionFit: A handsel is a gift for luck at the start of something, such as a coin placed in a new garment's pocket.

clue.text: Mansion's cold inside? Envious one responsible for rent

indicators.note: having something inside means one word holds the other within it

blocks.note: casa is the Spanish and Italian word for a house
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A grand house is freezing inside, and a jealous tenant is the one who pays the rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' is a tear, not a payment: in Julius Caesar, Antony shows the crowd 'what a rent the envious Casca made' in Caesar's cloak.
explanation.definitionFit: Casca was the conspirator Shakespeare calls envious, whose dagger made a tear in Caesar's mantle.

clue.text: Radio chat (vapid), producer-generated stuff

blocks.note: on air means broadcast on radio
gas is idle, empty talk

explanation.surface: Inane radio chatter is the stuff a programme producer churns out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Producer' suggests a radio producer; it is a gas producer, a furnace that makes fuel gas.
explanation.definitionFit: Air gas, or producer gas, is fuel gas made by blowing air through glowing coal or coke in a producer.

clue.text: Cliff (or Mark) firmly fixes ledges for Scotch

blocks.note: a scar is a steep rocky cliff, and also a mark left by a wound
to cement is to fix firmly

explanation.surface: The singers Cliff and Mark have firm hold of the ledges, while someone wants Scotch.
explanation.walkthrough: Cliff Richard prompts a person's name; it is a rock face. 'For Scotch' means the Scots word, not whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Scarcement is a Scots word for a ledge or set-back in a wall or bank.

clue.text: What'll spur purposeful behaviour, feasible in what's positively charged

indicators.note: one thing in another means it sits within the second word

blocks.note: a cation is an ion that is positively charged; 'what's' makes the phrase a noun
if a plan is on, it is feasible

explanation.surface: An incentive scheme seems feasible to an upbeat, highly charged manager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positively charged' reads as enthusiastic; in chemistry it describes a particle.
explanation.definitionFit: Conation is the faculty of will or striving that drives deliberate, goal-directed action, in psychology's term.

clue.text: Former champ's termination of bout, top-class?

indicators.note: a termination is an ending, so only the final letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: Muhammad Ali, former world heavyweight champion, with the 's
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: The end of a fight between former champions was boxing of the highest class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Termination of bout' sounds like a knockout; it takes only the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The A-list is the top category of celebrities or guests; the question mark admits it is a noun used for top-class.

clue.text: A bit of Georgia's money changeable for a rial

indicators.note: what is changeable can be altered, so these letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A Georgian coin that can be swapped at the bureau for a Middle Eastern rial.
explanation.walkthrough: A rial is a real currency, so the surface reads as an exchange rate; here it is only the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Laari is a variant spelling of lari, the monetary unit of Georgia; the clue's 'bit of' allows for a coin rather than the currency.

clue.text: Close friend, fellow grabbed by nursemaid showing passion for e.g. ASBOs

indicators.note: something grabbed by another is held within its grasp, so it goes inside

blocks.note: aia, or ayah, is a nursemaid in India
a crony is a close friend
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A nanny grabs a pal and a bloke, showing a mania for antisocial behaviour orders.
explanation.walkthrough: An ASBO was a UK Anti-Social Behaviour Order, an initialism of the sort the answer's mania loves.
explanation.definitionFit: Acronymania is an obsession with coining and using acronyms and abbreviations such as ASBO.

clue.text: Crystal, special company when in love

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits within the second word

blocks.note: love is a zero score, as in tennis
CO is the usual abbreviation for company; 'special' only colours the surface

explanation.surface: A lover gives a crystal to someone who has become special company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special' gets no letters of its own: it only qualifies the company that gives CO.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nicol is a prism cut from a calcite crystal, used to produce polarised light, and is named after its inventor William Nicol.

clue.text: Cancerous agent very little short of powerful, curtailed

indicators.note: curtailed means having had the tail cut off, so the final letter of that word goes

blocks.note: 'on' can mean very nearly, as in 'on fifty', a little short of a figure
a cogent argument is a powerful one

explanation.surface: A cancer-causing agent is only just short of being powerful, but has been cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very little short of' reads as part of a comparison; it means 'nearly', as 'on' does when a figure is approached.
explanation.definitionFit: An oncogene, or oncogen, is a gene or substance that can turn a normal cell cancerous.

clue.text: Cricketer made runs in singles?

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits within the second piece

blocks.note: two singles are two ones, written as the Roman numeral I twice
ran is the past tense of run

explanation.surface: A batsman piled up his runs one at a time, in singles.
explanation.walkthrough: Singles are ones; RAN goes between two I's. Ronnie Irani was an Essex and England all-rounder.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronnie Irani is a former England cricketer, so his surname answers to a cricketer.

clue.text: Carnival time — tipple knocked back before rag is arranged (9, two words)

indicators.note: knocked back means sent backwards, so the drink word is read from its end
arranged means put into an order, so these letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: a dram is a small drink of spirits
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: At carnival time a drink is downed before the students' rag parade is organised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back' looks like drinking the tipple, which is the surface joke; cryptically it reverses it. A rag is a British student charity carnival.
explanation.definitionFit: Mardi Gras, Shrove Tuesday, is the climax of the carnival season before Lent.

clue.text: Nutrition gone haywire: in short it's mash of hops and rye

indicators.note: in short means shortened, so the small word loses its opening letter
a mash is something pulped and mixed up, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, before shortening; its 's is just 'is'
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A brewer's mash of hops and rye has gone badly wrong for the diet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' shortened is the 't of 'tis, giving T; the hops and rye are then mashed after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Trophesy is a rare medical word for disordered nutrition of a part of the body, caused by nerve trouble.

clue.text: Losing one's cool at the wheel, an obstacle to progress with deer around (8, two words)

definitions.text: Losing one's cool at the wheel

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the deer word wraps the rest

blocks.note: a roe is a small deer
an is the indefinite article
a drag is a hindrance that slows progress

explanation.surface: A driver loses their temper when deer block the road ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: Road rage is a motorist's violent anger towards other road users, a loss of cool behind the wheel.

clue.text: E.g. Derby, just the thing? Get away! (8, two words)

blocks.note: Derby is an English cheese, so it is an example of one
'that's it' means that's just the thing wanted

explanation.surface: A punter hears the Derby described as just the thing, and replies in disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: Derby tempts the solver towards the horse race or the hat; it is the cheese from Derbyshire.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Cheese it!' is old slang meaning stop it or run off, used as an exclamation like 'get away!'.

clue.text: Wherein pupils learn for themselves, and sir — um — he's knocked off

indicators.note: something knocked off is roughly dashed out, so these letters are thrown into another order

blocks.note: the letters as written, ignoring dashes

explanation.surface: A hesitant schoolmaster gets dismissed while pupils teach themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of he's is 'is', linking the fodder to its indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Heurism is the teaching method in which pupils discover things for themselves, from Greek heuriskein, to find.

clue.text: Subject discussed on gardening programme? Listener enters card (7, two words)

indicators.note: to enter something is to go inside it

blocks.note: tose, or toze, is an old word meaning to tease or card wool
the ear is what listens

explanation.surface: A listener phones in with a card on a radio gardening show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listener' fits a radio audience; it is simply the organ of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea rose is a garden rose with a tea-like scent, just the sort of plant a gardening programme covers.

clue.text: Source of fodder, leafy, hid nuts

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so these letters run wild into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An animal's fodder, leafy stuff, in which nuts have been hidden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' reads as food stored in the leaves, which suits the fodder picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Hay grown in a field is cut and dried as winter feed for livestock, so the field is where that fodder comes from.

clue.text: Fill out staff attendance forms internally

indicators.note: internally means on the inside, so the letters lie inside the neighbouring words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of staff into attendance

explanation.surface: Office staff complete their attendance forms for internal use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fill out' and 'forms' suggest paperwork; fill out means grow plumper.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill out is to grow plumper, which is what fatten means.

clue.text: Goal is, deviously, to lampoon the Church in verse

definitions.text: to lampoon the Church in verse

indicators.note: deviously means by a winding, crooked path, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A satirist's devious aim is to mock the clergy in rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Golias, from the legendary goliard poet, is an old verb for writing satirical Latin verse against churchmen.

clue.text: Greek department — it's certainly not the majority failing to finish

indicators.note: failing to finish means stopping short, so the final letter is lost

blocks.note: no is an emphatic denial
most means the majority

explanation.surface: A Greek government department insists it is not where most people fail.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomos is one of the administrative provinces of modern Greece, also called a nome or prefecture.

clue.text: Writ resulting from coach reversing, one wrongly going into dad

indicators.note: a vehicle reversing goes backwards, so the coach word is read from the end
something done wrongly is out of order, so these letters are mixed
going into another word means sitting inside it

blocks.note: a coach is a long-distance bus
pa is an informal word for father
taken as written

explanation.surface: A court writ follows after a coach backed into somebody's father.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reversing' looks like a road accident; it turns the coach backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A subpoena is a writ ordering a person to attend court, under penalty for refusal.

clue.text: Overindulge

blocks.note: reading one: a bare definition, to eat or drink to excess
reading two: there is no wordplay, because this is the word readers write their own clues for

explanation.walkthrough: This is Azed's competition clue: the word is given by a bare definition and readers send in their own clues for it.
explanation.definitionFit: To go on a spree of excessive eating or drinking is exactly to overindulge, so the verb is a plain synonym.

clue.text: Descriptive of rhetoric spoken when curbing a riot, disorderly

indicators.note: disorderly means out of order, so these letters are rearranged
to curb something is to hold it in, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: oral means spoken rather than written
taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A speaker's fine rhetoric is used to restrain an unruly riot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disorderly' seems to describe the riot, and it does: it mixes those very letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Oratorial means relating to oratory, the art of public speaking and rhetoric.

clue.text: Gangster's lost and in penitentiary

indicators.note: what is lost is no longer there, so the following word drops out

blocks.note: a brigand is a bandit, an armed robber
the word itself, which is removed

explanation.surface: A gangster's case is lost and he ends up in prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And' looks like a joining word but it is the letters taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: A brig is a prison, originally one aboard a warship, so it serves for a penitentiary.

clue.text: It was worn by Scottish women, and lots in Thailand? The opposite

definitions.text: It was worn by Scottish women

indicators.note: in places one word within another, as the surface first reads it
the opposite of the stated order swaps which word goes inside and which goes around

blocks.note: lots means many
T is the international vehicle code for Thailand

explanation.surface: A garment once worn by Scotswomen, and plenty of them to be found in Thailand.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, lots go in Thailand; 'The opposite' puts Thailand inside lots instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A manty is the old Scots form of mantua, a loose gown formerly worn by women.

clue.text: Almost solicit beginnings of rudimentary organisms under lab conditions? (7, two words)

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short
beginnings are the first letters, so only the initials are kept

blocks.note: to solicit is to invite or ask for
the first letters of each word

explanation.surface: A scientist asks for some primitive life forms to grow in the laboratory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rudimentary organisms' sounds like the answer's subject matter, but only their first letters count.
explanation.definitionFit: In vitro, Latin 'in glass', describes processes carried out in test tubes or dishes rather than in a living body.

clue.text: Great Dane: what one might be without lead, that is given runs

indicators.note: the lead is the front letter, so going without it drops the first letter

blocks.note: a great dane, read as the breed, is a dog
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A Great Dane let off the lead is given a run.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great Dane' looks like the dog, and the wordplay uses that, but the definition is Ogier the Dane, a legendary paladin of Charlemagne.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogier the Dane is a hero of the Charlemagne romances, a great warrior of Danish origin.

clue.text: Pedestal, breadth unaltered

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for breadth
unaltered means as is, left just as it was

explanation.surface: A statue's pedestal keeps the same width as before.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestal is the base on which something stands, and a basis is likewise a foundation or support.

clue.text: Nets, in the main unspecified

blocks.note: the main is the open sea, as in the Spanish Main
n is the mathematician's unspecified number; here in the plural

explanation.surface: A trawler nets its catch somewhere out on the open sea.
explanation.walkthrough: SEAN is a variant of seine, to fish with a seine net, so 'Nets' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To sean is to catch fish with a seine, a large hanging net, so seans means nets.

clue.text: Dépêche Mode's losing supposed force, say when retiring

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken out, so those letters drop from the word
retiring means withdrawing backwards, so these words are read from the end

blocks.note: taken as written, with the s
od is the hypothetical natural force once proposed to explain mesmerism
e.g. means for example, as 'say' does
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'

explanation.surface: The band Depeche Mode are losing their power as they retire.
explanation.walkthrough: Depeche Mode looks like the band's name, but dépêche alone is the definition. MODES without OD leaves MES.
explanation.definitionFit: Dépêche is French for a dispatch or message, so it is a foreign-language equivalent.
